extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in business, aviation, and legal implications (journalists, industry observers, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: A news report covering a corporation's leadership change amid a safety crisis (Boeing's CEO firing after 737 Max crashes), explaining causes, reactions, and consequences. Useful for readers tracking corporate accountability, regulatory relations, and industry impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for new leadership to regain regulators' confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing said it decided it needed new leadership to regain the confidence of regulators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify CEO removal: when a leader's continued presence undermines regulatory certification or cooperation, replacing leadership is presented as necessary to restore regulator trust and move toward recertification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewed commitment to full transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The company promised a “renewed commitment to full transparency.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency is framed as a core remedy for the crisis—disclosing safety issues to regulators, airlines and the public is a criterion for improved corporate behavior. The article cites Boeing's pledge but notes skepticism from unions, victims' families, and lawmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize safety over profit and stock price
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics say Boeing shifted from engineering-driven culture to a top-down system prioritizing containing costs and maximizing profit — and driving the stock price higher — which contributed to problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criterion for evaluating corporate decisions: whether safety considerations were subordinated to profit objectives. Quotes from lawmakers and ex-employees are used as evidence that profit-driven priorities are a failure mode to be corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure of design changes to pilots and regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing had not told pilots about MCAS until after the Lion Air crash, and regulators at the FAA didn’t know much about it either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit communication of substantive aircraft design or control-system changes to pilots and regulators is presented as a necessary standard. Failure to inform is cited as a contributing factor to crashes and subsequent loss of trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough technical investigation and fixing of root causes before resuming service
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘As long as they figured out what caused the crashes and they can solve that, then I’m fine with that,’ a passenger said; investigators point to MCAS and faulty sensors as causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article implies that reauthorization to fly should follow a complete technical fix and verification of root causes (e.g., MCAS and sensor reliability). This functions as an evaluative standard for when the fleet can safely return to service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repair and cooperation with aviation authorities (FAA and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: To rebuild trust, Boeing has to repair its relationship with the FAA and other authorities and must be transparent with the traveling public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoring institutional relationships with regulators—demonstrated cooperation, responsiveness, and credible remediation—is a criterion for recovery and regaining operating privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate accountability and accepting responsibility for mishandling accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Muilenburg was faulted for Boeing’s initial response to the accidents, when he and the company blamed the foreign pilots; criticism grew as internal documents revealed concerns about key design features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting responsibility (not blaming others) and addressing internal failures transparently is presented as a standard for appropriate crisis leadership. The article uses this to explain why calls for resignation or removal mounted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Halt production when deliverability or safety status is unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: It announced it would temporarily halt production of the Max because it wasn’t clear when it could deliver the planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporarily stopping production in face of grounded fleet and uncertain recertification is described as an operational criterion to avoid building undeliverable or unsafe aircraft and to control financial/exposure risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate customers and mitigate downstream impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing has estimated it will spend at least $9 billion to compensate airlines and adjust the Max production schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate financial remediation to airlines and partners affected by groundings and cancellations is presented as an expected corporate obligation and metric of the company's response adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address corporate culture shift back toward engineering and safety mindset
rubrics_metrics.description: The Max debacle has put the spotlight on Boeing’s culture, which some current and former employees say changed from one driven by engineering to a top-down management system focused on costs and profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term remedy requires cultural change: re-emphasizing engineering judgment and safety over cost-cutting and short-term shareholder returns. The article treats cultural reform as necessary for preventing recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent communication with the traveling public to rebuild consumer confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing must be transparent with the traveling public; passengers’ willingness to fly the Max depends on confidence that causes were found and fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-facing communications and demonstrable fixes are criteria for restoring passenger confidence; consumer acceptance is an outcome measure of effective remediation and messaging.
